title: Rule of Law and Rule by Law
text:
The phrase “rule of law” is used so often that its meaning can seem obvious. It is sometimes taken to mean simply that a country has laws and enforces them. But every government, including the most oppressive, issues laws. A regime may pass a decree banning criticism and then prosecute its critics with perfect legal formality. That is rule by law: law used as an instrument of power. The rule of law means something more demanding.

At its core is the principle that no one is above the law. Those who make and enforce the rules must themselves be bound by them. A minister who breaks the law should face the same courts as an ordinary citizen, and a government that wishes to act must be able to point to legal authority for doing so.

Several conditions follow from this principle. Laws should be public, so that people know what is expected of them; they should be reasonably clear and stable, rather than changed overnight to suit the powerful; and they should not punish actions retrospectively. Above all, disputes must be decided by independent judges who can rule against the government without fear of dismissal.

These conditions matter to ordinary life as much as to politics. A farmer who cannot be sure that his title to his land will be respected has little reason to invest in it; a trader who cannot enforce a contract will deal only with his relatives. Where the rule of law is weak, trust shrinks to the circle of family and friends, and both freedom and prosperity suffer.

title: The Press and the Citizen
text:
Democracy rests on the assumption that citizens can make informed choices. They elect representatives, judge policies and hold officials to account. None of this is possible without reliable information about what those in power are doing. For this reason, a free press has long been described as the eyes and ears of the public, reporting on matters that ordinary people have neither the time nor the access to investigate themselves.

Good journalism is costly. Investigating a corrupt contract may take months of interviews, document searches and legal checks before a single line is published. Traditionally, newspapers paid for such work through sales and advertising. As readers and advertisers have moved online, many outlets have lost much of that income. Local reporting, which covers councils, courts and schools, has often been the first casualty.

The consequences are subtle but serious. When no reporter attends council meetings, officials face less scrutiny, and some research has suggested that local government becomes more costly where local newspapers close. At the same time, the gap is filled by an abundance of opinion and rumour online, much of it unverified and designed to confirm what audiences already believe.

A healthy democracy therefore needs more than freedom of expression. It needs institutions that can afford to find and check facts, and citizens willing to support them. Paying for good journalism, whether through subscriptions or through public funding with safeguards for independence, may be as important to self-government as the right to vote itself.

title: Speed Versus Truth
text:
Within minutes of any disaster, the rumours begin. A photograph from another country is shared as evidence of local destruction; a message claiming that a dam has burst travels faster than any official statement; an unverified list of casualties circulates before families have been informed. By the time the facts are established, thousands of people may have acted on falsehoods, fleeing safe areas, clogging roads or hoarding supplies.

It would be easy to blame technology alone. But messaging applications merely accelerate an old human impulse. In moments of fear, people want to know something, and they want to warn those they love. Sharing a dramatic message feels like an act of care. Unfortunately, good intentions do not make false information any less harmful.

The authorities bear part of the responsibility. When official channels are slow, vague or silent, they leave a vacuum that rumour quickly fills. Emergency agencies should publish short, frequent updates, even if the update is only that information is still being gathered. Admitting uncertainty honestly builds more trust than silence followed by a late announcement.

Citizens, too, have a duty. Before forwarding an alarming message, each of us should ask a few simple questions. Who wrote it? Is it dated? Has any recognised source confirmed it? In a crisis, pausing for a moment is not indifference; it is a form of responsibility. The speed at which we share should never outrun our concern for whether what we share is true.

title: The Trap of Sunk Costs
text:
Imagine a man who has bought an expensive ticket for a concert. On the evening of the performance he feels unwell and a heavy storm is raging, yet he drags himself out because, as he puts it, he has already paid. His money, however, is gone whether he goes or not. The only real question is whether the evening will be better spent at the concert or at home. By allowing a past expense to govern a present choice, he has fallen into what economists call the sunk-cost fallacy.

The error is remarkably common and far from limited to individuals. Companies continue to fund failing projects because so much has already been invested; governments persist with costly schemes long after their flaws are clear, partly because abandoning them would seem to admit that earlier spending was wasted. The more that has been spent, the stronger the temptation to spend more in the hope of rescuing it.

Psychologists offer several explanations. People dislike losses more than they value equivalent gains, and walking away makes a loss feel final. They also wish to appear consistent, both to others and to themselves. Changing course can look like weakness, even when it is the wiser choice.

The remedy is simple to state but hard to practise: decisions should look forward, not back. The useful question is not “How much have we put in?” but “Given where we stand now, which course offers the best results from here?” Those who learn to ask it may occasionally have to accept an uncomfortable loss, but they avoid the far greater cost of throwing good resources after bad.

subject: English
q: The main purpose of the passage is to:
o: describe how laws are drafted by parliaments
distinguish the rule of law from the mere use of law by those in power
argue that oppressive governments have no laws
explain the procedure for dismissing judges
explanation: The passage contrasts “rule by law”, law as an instrument of power, with the more demanding rule of law and explains what the latter requires.

subject: English
q: According to the passage, the core principle of the rule of law is that:
o: no one is above the law
laws should be changed frequently
judges should obey the government
every government must issue decrees
explanation: The second paragraph says that at its core is the principle that no one is above the law.

subject: English
q: Which of the following does the passage list as a condition that follows from the rule of law?
o: Judges should be appointed by the ruling party
Laws should be adjusted quickly to suit those in power
Ministers should be tried in special courts
Laws should be public so that people know what is expected of them
explanation: The third paragraph lists public, clear and stable laws, no retrospective punishment and independent judges; the other options contradict these conditions.

subject: English
q: The word ‘retrospectively’, as used in the passage, most nearly means:
o: harshly and without mercy
in a way that applies to actions done before the law was made
only after a public trial
secretly and without explanation
explanation: Laws should not punish actions retrospectively, that is, they should not reach back to punish conduct that was lawful when it was done.

subject: English
q: The examples of the farmer and the trader suggest that where the rule of law is weak:
o: families benefit because business stays among relatives
only politicians and ministers are affected
farmers are encouraged to buy more land
investment is discouraged and trust is limited to close relations
explanation: The farmer has little reason to invest and the trader deals only with relatives; the author concludes that trust shrinks and prosperity suffers.

subject: English
q: The author’s tone in the passage is best described as:
o: emotional and outraged
humorous and mocking
explanatory and reasoned
doubtful and hesitant
explanation: The author defines a concept step by step, lists its conditions and illustrates their practical importance in a calm, reasoned manner.

subject: English
q: Which of the following is the most appropriate title for the passage?
o: Why Democracy Needs Reliable Journalism
The Decline of Printed Books
How to Write a Newspaper Column
Online Opinion as a Substitute for News
explanation: The passage argues that informed citizenship depends on costly, reliable reporting and that such journalism must be paid for.

subject: English
q: According to the passage, what has often been the first casualty of falling newspaper income?
o: Coverage of international affairs
Local reporting on councils, courts and schools
Opinion columns and editorials
Online advertising revenue
explanation: The second paragraph says local reporting, which covers councils, courts and schools, has often been the first casualty.

subject: English
q: Why, according to the passage, is investigative journalism costly?
o: Reporters must pay officials for information
Stories must be printed in several languages
Advertisers insist on checking every story
It may take months of interviews, document searches and legal checks
explanation: The passage says investigating a corrupt contract may take months of interviews, document searches and legal checks before anything is published.

subject: English
q: The word ‘scrutiny’, as used in the passage, most nearly means:
o: close examination
public support
legal protection
financial pressure
explanation: When no reporter attends council meetings, officials are watched less closely; scrutiny means careful examination.

subject: English
q: It can be inferred that the author regards online opinion and rumour as:
o: an adequate replacement for local newspapers
the main source of newspapers’ income
a guarantee of closer scrutiny of officials
a poor substitute for verified reporting
explanation: The author says the gap left by local news is filled by opinion and rumour that is largely unverified and designed to confirm existing beliefs.

subject: English
q: In the final paragraph, the author compares paying for journalism with the right to vote in order to:
o: stress how essential reliable information is to self-government
suggest that voting should be replaced by subscriptions
argue that journalists should stand for election
show that public funding always threatens independence
explanation: By ranking support for journalism alongside the vote, the author emphasises that democracy cannot work without reliable information.

subject: English
q: The main point of the editorial is that during emergencies:
o: messaging applications should be shut down completely
people should never warn their relatives of danger
both authorities and citizens must act to check the spread of false information
official statements are usually less reliable than rumours
explanation: The editorial assigns responsibility to the authorities, who should update frequently, and to citizens, who should check messages before sharing them.

subject: English
q: According to the passage, why do people share dramatic messages in a crisis?
o: They are paid to spread rumours
They distrust all modern technology
They want to know something and to warn those they love
They wish to embarrass the authorities
explanation: The second paragraph says that in moments of fear people want to know something and to warn those they love.

subject: English
q: What does the writer advise emergency agencies to do?
o: Publish short, frequent updates even while facts are still being gathered
Wait until every fact is confirmed before making any statement
Block all private messages during disasters
Leave public communication to citizens’ groups
explanation: The third paragraph urges short, frequent updates, even if the update is only that information is still being gathered.

subject: English
q: The word ‘vacuum’, as used in the passage, most nearly means:
o: a strict official rule
an empty space left by an absence
a sudden wave of panic
a formal public statement
explanation: Slow or silent official channels leave a vacuum that rumour fills, that is, a gap created by the absence of information.

subject: English
q: The writer’s statement that ‘pausing for a moment is not indifference’ implies that:
o: people who share messages quickly do not care about others
checking a message before sharing it shows concern rather than a lack of care
citizens should ignore every alarming message
indifference is the best response to a crisis
explanation: Since sharing feels like an act of care, the writer reassures readers that pausing to verify is itself a responsible, caring act.

subject: English
q: The tone of the editorial is best described as:
o: earnest and persuasive
detached and indifferent
flippant and humorous
despairing and resigned
explanation: The writer seriously urges both authorities and citizens to act, using direct appeals such as “each of us should ask”.

subject: English
q: The passage chiefly warns against:
o: buying concert tickets in advance
letting past expenses determine present decisions
admitting mistakes in public
investing in any long-term project
explanation: The passage describes the sunk-cost fallacy, allowing a past expense to govern a present choice, and recommends forward-looking decisions.

subject: English
q: According to the passage, why might a government persist with a costly scheme?
o: Abandoning it would seem to admit that earlier spending was wasted
The scheme’s flaws have not yet become clear
Citizens demand that every scheme be completed
Economists advise finishing all projects
explanation: The second paragraph says governments persist partly because abandoning a scheme would seem to admit that earlier spending was wasted.

subject: English
q: Which explanation of the sunk-cost fallacy does the passage attribute to psychologists?
o: People feel losses more strongly than equivalent gains
People enjoy taking financial risks
People forget how much they have spent
People trust experts more than themselves
explanation: The third paragraph says people dislike losses more than they value equivalent gains, and walking away makes a loss feel final.

subject: English
q: The word ‘persist’, as used in the passage, most nearly means:
o: hesitate briefly
continue firmly
refuse openly
complain loudly
explanation: Governments persist with schemes long after their flaws are clear, meaning they carry on with them despite reasons to stop.

subject: English
q: Which of the following decisions would the author consider sound?
o: Finishing a disliked meal because it was expensive
Stopping a failing project after judging that further spending will not pay off
Completing a failing building because much has already been spent on it
Keeping a bad investment to avoid appearing inconsistent
explanation: The author says decisions should ask which course offers the best results from here; the other options let past spending or a wish for consistency decide.

subject: English
q: The author’s tone in the passage is best described as:
o: angry and accusing
analytical and advisory
nostalgic and sentimental
sarcastic and dismissive
explanation: The author analyses the causes of a common error and ends with practical advice on how to avoid it.
